content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
A type describes which values an object can represent and which operations are meaningful. Prefer initialization at the declaration and use explicit conversions when information could be lost.

Type Modifiers and Type Qualifiers focuses on the decisions and observable behavior named by the subtopics below. The aim is to explain the rule, predict what a small program should do, and then confirm the result with a focused check.

Write down the range and meaning of each value before choosing a type; test boundary values and compile with warnings enabled.

items.title: signed and unsigned
items.text: Signed and unsigned integers have different ranges and mixed comparisons can surprise; choose types by meaning and validate conversions.

items.title: short and long
items.text: Explain short and long in the context of Type Modifiers and Type Qualifiers: identify the rule, trace a minimal example, and check one boundary or failure case.

items.title: The const Qualifier
items.text: const prevents modification through that particular access path; it does not automatically make pointed-to data or every reachable object immutable.

items.title: The volatile Qualifier
items.text: volatile is for specific observable accesses, not inter-thread synchronization; use atomics or locks to coordinate threads.

items.title: The constexpr Specifier
items.text: constexpr allows an entity or function to participate in constant evaluation when its use satisfies the language rules.

items.title: The consteval Specifier
items.text: consteval declares an immediate function whose invocations must be evaluated at compile time under the language rules.

items.title: The constinit Specifier
items.text: constinit requires static or thread-local initialization to be constant initialization; it does not make the variable const.

content.task: Create a small, independent example that demonstrates type modifiers and type qualifiers. Predict the result before compiling, write down a precondition, and test one ordinary case plus one boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example builds under a documented standard mode with warnings enabled.
The predicted and observed result are recorded; deviations are explained.
At least one boundary, invalid-input, lifetime or portability assumption is tested or documented.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming one successful example proves every case.
common_mistakes.why: It may miss an invalid input, boundary, error path or implementation difference.
common_mistakes.fix: Write down the preconditions and test at least one ordinary case plus an edge or failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a language feature without checking its requirements.
common_mistakes.why: The code may depend on a standard version, an object lifetime or an API precondition.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the explicit standard mode and verify the relevant rule and compiler/library support.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring compiler diagnostics or simplifying away ownership and error behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Warnings and explicit contracts often expose a defect before it becomes a runtime problem.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile with warnings, keep the smallest reproducible sample and state what happens when an operation fails.
